scenes.heading: Fundamental Mechanisms
scenes.visual_text: Ionic: charged ions attract | Covalent: shared pairs bind
scenes.narration: What is the difference between ionic and covalent bonding? Both arise from electrical attractions that lower the combined system’s energy, but they organize electrons differently. Ionic bonding relies on oppositely charged ions. Covalent bonding holds atoms together through shared electron pairs.

scenes.heading: Ionic Lattices
scenes.visual_text: Na → Cl transfer | Na⁺ ↔ Cl⁻ lattice
scenes.narration: In a simplified ionic picture, sodium transfers an electron to chlorine. Sodium becomes positively charged and chlorine becomes negatively charged. Their opposite charges attract throughout a repeating crystal lattice, as in table salt.

scenes.heading: Covalent Sharing
scenes.visual_text: H–H electron density cloud | Attracted to both nuclei
scenes.narration: In a covalent bond, atoms share electron density. In a hydrogen molecule, one shared pair is attracted to both nuclei. Covalent bonds commonly join nonmetal atoms into distinct molecules or network structures.

scenes.heading: Macroscopic Properties
scenes.visual_text: Ionic: brittle, high-melting, conduct when mobile | Covalent: varied melting, usually insulating
scenes.narration: Ionic compounds are often crystalline, brittle, and high-melting. They conduct electricity when melted or dissolved because ions can move. Molecular covalent substances often melt lower and usually do not conduct, though exceptions matter.

scenes.heading: The Bonding Continuum
scenes.visual_text: Lattice of ions ↔ Shared electron density
scenes.narration: Use the models as a continuum, not two perfect boxes. Many bonds have both ionic and covalent character. The practical distinction is whether we describe a lattice of ions or atoms sharing electron density.
